To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

the malignant conversion of rat liver epithelial cells is accompanied by a decreased expression of surface fibronectin in conjunction with the increased expression of a 140-kilodalton species and of a 60-kilodalton component.

malignant transformation is associated with the loss of fibronectin from the surface of liver epithelial cells and that arginine deprivation leads to the loss of fibroblast-like surface proteins from both normal and malignant cells, with the malignant cells being more sensitive to arginine deprivation than the normal ones.

the expression of fibronectin on the surfaces of normal liver epithelium cells is decreased in malignant liver epithelial cell counterparts, and that this decrease can be reversed by arginine addition to the culture medium of the transformed cells.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the identification of cell surface changes in normal and malignant liver cells.

the study of the molecular mechanisms of malignant transformation of normal liver epithelia, with the identification of the molecular alterations that occur during the process and with the analysis of the role played by arginine in the expression and maintenance of the transformed phenotype.
the study of liver cell transformation, a process that is of interest for its relevance to the etiology of liver cancer, the third most frequent human neoplasm.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
fibronectin is a normal cell-surface protein that is decreased in malignant cells and that is regulated by arginine availability.

the cell surface macromolecular changes that accompany the malignant transformation of rat liver epithelial cells include the expression of a 140K-dalton component that appears to be a specific marker for the malignant phenotype.

the surface labeling of the normal liver epithelial cell surface with the anti-fibronactin antiserum led to the recognition of the 240,000-daltons fibronectin molecule, while in the malignant liver cell counterpart, a 140, 000-dalton and a 60,000 dalton component were labeled in preference to the fibronectins.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

arginine limitation is a growth-inhibitory agent that induces a number of changes in cell surface molecules, some of them being common to normal and tumorigenic liver cell counterparts, whereas other surface macromolecular changes are specific for normal or malignant cells.
arginine limitation is a growth-arrest signal in normal and malignant liver cells.

the expression of fibronectin by liver epithelial cells is under the control of arginine availability and that malignant conversion is associated with the loss of arginine-regulated expression of fibronactin.
The main takeaway from our work is that

the surface of the normal liver epithelial cell is rich in fibronectin (and other proteins), and that the surface of malignant cells is different, with a decreased level of fibronectin but an increased level of a 140-kDa protein.

the cell surface of normal and transformed liver epithelial cells is composed of a complex mixture of macromolecules, some of which are shared with the fibroblasts and others that are specific for the epithelial cell type.
the cell surface macromolecular profile of a cell is not only a reflection of the genetic state of the cell but also of the metabolic state of the cell.
